items.prompt: GreenCart's checkout service passed every load test and returned correct responses throughout the flash sale, yet the team still treated the resulting bill as a real problem. Which idea best explains why?
choices: Load tests don't measure correctness, only speed
Cost is a non-functional requirement, like latency or availability — a design that's economically unsustainable has still failed, just on a slower clock than an outage
The team should have used a different cloud provider
Correct systems never have cost problems, so this must have been a billing error
items.explanation: Availability and latency failures show up in monitoring within seconds; cost failures show up on a monthly invoice. Both are still requirements the design either meets or doesn't — 'it worked' isn't the whole bar if it worked at a cost the business can't sustain as it grows.
items.reference:
✅ Correct + fast + available
💸 ...but costs more per unit as it grows

Why: cost is a non-functional requirement alongside latency and availability — it just fails on the invoice's clock, not the monitor's.

items.prompt: A team ships a feature that's fast, correct, and passes every review — but its cost per active user triples within a month of launch. Is this an architecture problem?
choices: No — cost is a finance/procurement concern, not an architecture one
Yes — cost is a non-functional requirement alongside latency and availability, and a design that's unsustainable to run has failed even if it's functionally correct
No — as long as the company can afford the bill, cost is irrelevant to the design
Yes, but only if the system also becomes measurably slower
items.explanation: Whether the company can currently afford it and whether the design is sound are different questions. A rising cost per user is the same kind of signal as rising latency under load: the design isn't holding up as the system scales, and that's an architecture problem regardless of the current bank balance.
items.reference:
✅ Correct + fast + available
💸 ...but costs more per unit as it grows

Why: cost is a non-functional requirement alongside latency and availability — it just fails on the invoice's clock, not the monitor's.

items.prompt: GreenCart's total cloud bill went from $800 to $9,600 (12x) while revenue went from $80K to $480K (6x). Which single number best captures why this was treated as a problem, rather than just 'the bill went up because we grew'?
choices: Total spend increased at all
Cost per order roughly tripled ($0.04 to $0.11) — the system got economically less efficient as it grew, not just bigger
Revenue grew slower than expected in absolute dollars
The bill exceeded $10,000 for the first time
items.explanation: Total spend rising is expected during growth, and on its own tells you nothing about whether the architecture is holding up. Cost per order tripling is the actionable signal — it means each additional order is more expensive to serve than the last, which is the opposite of what should happen as volume grows.
items.reference:
Total spendcan rise and be fine
Cost/unitrising is the warning sign

Why: the metric that matters is cost per unit of value, not total spend.

items.prompt: A SaaS company's total infrastructure cost doubles as its active users double over a quarter. Cost per active user stays flat. Should this be treated as a cost problem?
choices: Yes, doubling any cost is inherently concerning
Not on its own — cost per user staying flat while total cost doubles alongside users is expected and healthy; the concern would be if cost per user had risen
No, total spend is the only number that matters, and it's fine as long as it's growing
Yes, because infra cost should always grow slower than revenue in absolute dollars, regardless of the ratio
items.explanation: Total cost scaling with total users, at a flat rate per user, is exactly what a healthy architecture looks like. The metric to watch is the per-unit number, not the total — a flat or falling cost per user alongside a rising total is the system behaving correctly under growth.
items.reference:
Total spendcan rise and be fine
Cost/unitrising is the warning sign

Why: the metric that matters is cost per unit of value, not total spend.

items.prompt: A data pipeline's total storage bill grows every month as more data arrives. Which additional number turns 'the bill went up' into an actionable signal?
choices: The number of engineers on the team
Cost per GB stored/processed — whether the unit cost is flat, falling, or rising as volume grows
The total number of tables in the warehouse
How many dashboards reference the data
items.explanation: As with orders and active users, the raw total tells you the pipeline is being used more — expected. Cost per GB tells you whether that usage is getting cheaper, flat, or more expensive to serve per unit, which is the number that actually points at an architecture decision worth making.
items.reference:
Total spendcan rise and be fine
Cost/unitrising is the warning sign

Why: the metric that matters is cost per unit of value, not total spend.

items.prompt: Which pair correctly matches 'fixed cost' and 'variable cost' to real examples from a cloud bill?
choices: Fixed: an API call metered per request. Variable: a 1-year reserved instance.
Fixed: a 1-year reserved instance running whether or not it's used. Variable: usage-metered compute and per-request database calls.
Fixed and variable are just two different names for the same thing
Fixed: anything under $1,000/month. Variable: anything over $1,000/month.
items.explanation: Fixed cost is paid regardless of usage — a committed instance running at 3am with no traffic still costs the same. Variable cost scales directly with usage — a per-request DB call or metered API charge only accrues when the request actually happens.
items.reference:
💰 Fixed: paid whether used or not
📈 Variable: scales with usage

Why: which lever helps depends on which part of the bill is out of control.

items.prompt: A team reserves a database cluster for 3 years at a flat monthly rate, and separately pays a metered rate per API call to a third-party fraud-detection service. Which cost is fixed and which is variable?
choices: Both are variable, since both show up on a monthly bill
The reserved cluster is fixed (paid regardless of usage); the metered fraud-detection API is variable (scales directly with call volume)
The reserved cluster is variable; the metered API is fixed
Neither is fixed or variable — that distinction only applies to compute, not storage or third-party APIs
items.explanation: The reserved cluster's cost doesn't move whether it handles 10 calls or 10 million this month — that's fixed. The fraud-detection API's bill moves directly with call volume — that's variable, and the distinction applies to any metered cost, not just compute.
items.reference:
💰 Fixed: paid whether used or not
📈 Variable: scales with usage

Why: which lever helps depends on which part of the bill is out of control.

items.prompt: Which pricing model typically offers the deepest discount, in exchange for the workload being interruptible and retry-safe?
choices: Reserved / committed-use
Spot / preemptible
On-demand
Serverless
items.explanation: Spot/preemptible capacity is unused capacity the provider can reclaim at any time — because the provider can take it back, it's priced at the deepest discount (often 60-90% off on-demand), but only workloads that tolerate interruption and can retry safely should run on it.
items.reference:
ModelDiscount
On-demand0%
Reserved30-70%
Spot60-90%

Why: the right model depends on how predictable and interruptible the workload is, not just the listed discount.

items.prompt: A workload has near-zero baseline traffic most of the day, with occasional bursts triggered by user activity. Which pricing model is typically the best starting fit?
choices: Reserved / committed-use, sized to the burst
On-demand only, never autoscaled
Serverless (pay-per-invocation)
Spot, because bursts are short
items.explanation: Serverless charges per invocation with no idle baseline cost — exactly the right shape for a workload that's near-zero most of the day and bursty on top. Reserving capacity sized to the burst would mean paying for idle capacity the rest of the day.
items.reference:
ModelDiscount
On-demand0%
Reserved30-70%
Spot60-90%

Why: the right model depends on how predictable and interruptible the workload is, not just the listed discount.

items.prompt: Which pricing model requires no upfront commitment and charges the full, undiscounted baseline rate?
choices: On-demand
Reserved / committed-use
Spot / preemptible
All models charge the same baseline rate
items.explanation: On-demand is the baseline every other model is discounted against — no commitment, no discount, but also no risk of paying for unused reserved capacity or losing spot capacity mid-task.
items.reference:
ModelDiscount
On-demand0%
Reserved30-70%
Spot60-90%

Why: the right model depends on how predictable and interruptible the workload is, not just the listed discount.

items.prompt: Which of the following is most likely to be missing from an architecture diagram, yet still show up as a significant line item on the cloud bill?
choices: The name of the primary database
Cross-region or egress data transfer between services
The programming language used
The number of Git branches in the repo
items.explanation: Data transfer between regions or out to the internet doesn't get drawn as a box on a diagram — it's an arrow, at best — but providers meter it, and at volume it's routinely one of the largest line items on a real bill.
items.reference:
🌐 Egress / cross-region transfer
💤 Idle 'just in case' capacity
📊 Observability ingestion
🔌 Metered third-party APIs

Why: none of these are boxes on a diagram, but all of them are line items on the invoice.

items.prompt: A team's logging setup ships every request's full payload to a third-party observability platform, priced per GB ingested. Six months later, observability is the second-largest line item on the bill. What category of cost does this best illustrate?
choices: A pricing model choice, like reserved vs. on-demand
A hidden/easy-to-miss cost that doesn't appear as a box on an architecture diagram but still accumulates
A one-time migration cost
A cost that only affects total spend, never cost per request
items.explanation: Observability ingestion is a textbook hidden cost: it's a byproduct of every request, scales with request volume just like the request itself, and rarely appears as a labeled component in a system's architecture diagram — until the bill forces attention to it.
items.reference:
🌐 Egress / cross-region transfer
💤 Idle 'just in case' capacity
📊 Observability ingestion
🔌 Metered third-party APIs

Why: none of these are boxes on a diagram, but all of them are line items on the invoice.

items.prompt: Which two architectural levers does this unit identify as the highest-leverage for reducing cost in most systems?
choices: Switching cloud providers and renegotiating contracts
Caching (avoiding a paid compute/DB call) and right-sizing (not paying for unused capacity)
Hiring a dedicated FinOps team and buying more reserved instances
Reducing logging and increasing replica count
items.explanation: Caching turns a paid downstream call into a free cache hit; right-sizing stops paying for capacity nothing is using. Both attack cost directly at the architecture level, without depending on contract negotiation or organizational change.
items.reference:
🗄️ Caching → fewer paid downstream calls
📏 Right-sizing → no paying for unused capacity

Why: both act directly on the formula's variable and fixed terms.

items.prompt: In costPerRequest(requests) = (fixedCost / requests) + variableCostPerRequest, what happens to costPerRequest as requests grows, assuming variableCostPerRequest is truly constant?
choices: It rises without bound
It approaches variableCostPerRequest from above, since fixedCost/requests shrinks toward zero as requests grows
It stays exactly equal to fixedCost forever
It becomes undefined once requests exceeds fixedCost
items.explanation: The fixedCost/requests term is the only part of the formula that changes with volume, and it shrinks toward zero as requests grows — leaving costPerRequest converging on the flat variableCostPerRequest. This is economies of scale, falling straight out of the arithmetic.
items.reference:
costPerRequest = (fixedCost / requests) + variableCostPerRequest

Why: as requests grows, the fixed term dilutes toward zero on its own.

items.prompt: A system's fixedCost is $5,000/month and variableCostPerRequest is a true constant of $0.0002. At 1,000,000 requests/month, roughly what is costPerRequest?
choices: $0.0052 (fixedCost/requests = $0.005, plus $0.0002 variable)
$0.005 exactly, with no variable component
items.explanation: fixedCost/requests = 5000/1,000,000 = $0.005. Adding the constant variableCostPerRequest of $0.0002 gives $0.0052 total per request — both terms of the formula contribute, not just one.
items.reference:
costPerRequest = (fixedCost / requests) + variableCostPerRequest

Why: as requests grows, the fixed term dilutes toward zero on its own.

items.prompt: Why does L2 call the falling-cost-per-request curve 'economies of scale' the default, healthy shape rather than something that requires special effort?
choices: Because cloud providers automatically lower list prices as usage grows
Because it falls out of the formula automatically whenever variableCostPerRequest is genuinely flat — the fixed-cost term dilutes on its own as volume rises
Because it only happens if a team actively renegotiates its contract every quarter
Because total spend always falls as volume grows
items.explanation: No special intervention is needed for the curve to fall — it's a direct consequence of dividing a fixed number by a growing number. The special effort is needed to keep variableCostPerRequest genuinely flat as volume grows, not to make the curve fall in the first place.
items.reference:
costPerRequest = (fixedCost / requests) + variableCostPerRequest

Why: as requests grows, the fixed term dilutes toward zero on its own.

items.prompt: GreenCart's cost per order rose with volume instead of falling. Per L2, what does this reveal about their variableCostPerRequest?
choices: It was zero
It wasn't actually constant — it grew with volume, because contention on an un-cached, on-demand-only database increased as concurrent load rose
It was miscalculated by finance
Their fixedCost was too high
items.explanation: The formula only predicts a falling curve when variableCostPerRequest is genuinely flat. GreenCart's per-request DB write made variable cost rise with contention as volume grew, which is exactly what turns the formula's default falling curve into a rising one.
items.reference:
🗄️ DB write on every request, no cache
📈 Contention rises with concurrent load

Why: a 'constant' variable cost stops being constant once the underlying resource gets contended.

items.prompt: Which change to Service A would most directly address a variableCostPerRequest that grows with volume (rather than a fixedCost that's too small)?
choices: Reserving more baseline instances
Adding a cache in front of the database so most requests never generate DB load in the first place
Switching to a more expensive on-demand instance type
Increasing the number of read replicas without limit
items.explanation: Reserving more baseline capacity addresses fixedCost, not the rising variable term. A cache attacks the actual problem — it removes load from the database before it ever becomes a per-request cost, keeping variableCostPerRequest flat as volume grows.
items.reference:
🗄️ DB write on every request, no cache
📈 Contention rises with concurrent load

Why: a 'constant' variable cost stops being constant once the underlying resource gets contended.

items.prompt: In L2's chart comparing Service A and Service B, Service A's line rises left-to-right while Service B's falls. What does a rising cost-per-order line, as volume increases, indicate about that service's architecture?
choices: The service is becoming more efficient at scale
The service has diseconomies of scale — each additional order is proportionally more expensive to serve than the last
The service's total spend is decreasing
The chart indicates a pricing model change, not an architecture issue
items.explanation: A rising cost-per-unit line is the visual signature of diseconomies of scale: growth is making the system less efficient, not more, which is the opposite of what a sound architecture should do as volume increases.
items.reference:
Falling line = economies of scale (healthy)
Rising line = diseconomies of scale (warning)

Why: the direction of the cost-per-unit curve is the architecture's report card at scale.

items.prompt: Two services start at nearly the same cost per order at low volume, but diverge sharply as volume grows 10x. What does this tell you about comparing architectures using cost data collected only at low, early-stage volume?
choices: Early-stage cost-per-unit numbers are just as reliable as at-scale numbers
Early-stage cost-per-unit numbers can look similar for architectures that will diverge sharply at scale — the shape of the curve matters more than a single low-volume snapshot
Cost per unit is meaningless below 1M requests/month
Diverging curves always indicate a bug in one of the services
items.explanation: At low volume, the fixed-cost term dominates for both services regardless of how their variable cost behaves, which can mask a diseconomies-of-scale design until volume rises enough for the variable term to dominate. The curve's shape, not one snapshot, is what actually predicts behavior at scale.
items.reference:
Falling line = economies of scale (healthy)
Rising line = diseconomies of scale (warning)

Why: the direction of the cost-per-unit curve is the architecture's report card at scale.

items.prompt: Per L2's decision framework, a workload with roughly steady, predictable load should default to which pricing model for its baseline?
choices: Spot / preemptible
Reserved / committed-use capacity
Serverless only
Whichever option has the cheapest listed per-hour rate, regardless of predictability
items.explanation: Reserved capacity's discount is earned by committing in advance — which only pays off when the load is predictable enough that the commitment is actually used, exactly the case for steady, known baseline traffic.
items.reference:
Steady load → reserved · Interruptible → spot · Near-zero baseline → serverless · Otherwise → on-demand + autoscale

Why: the right model depends on predictability and interruption-tolerance, not just listed price.

items.prompt: A batch job reprocesses data nightly, can be safely restarted from a checkpoint if interrupted, and isn't latency-sensitive. Which pricing model is the framework's best fit?
choices: Reserved / committed-use
On-demand, never interrupted
Spot / preemptible — it's interruption-tolerant and retry-safe, which is exactly what spot pricing requires
Serverless, sized for the largest possible dataset
items.explanation: Spot capacity can be reclaimed at any time in exchange for a deep discount — a workload that tolerates interruption and can resume from a checkpoint is precisely the case that discount is designed for, with no downside from the reclaim risk.
items.reference:
Steady load → reserved · Interruptible → spot · Near-zero baseline → serverless · Otherwise → on-demand + autoscale

Why: the right model depends on predictability and interruption-tolerance, not just listed price.

items.prompt: A workload has near-zero baseline traffic most of the day, spiking only occasionally. Per the framework, which model fits best?
choices: Reserved capacity sized to the spike, running 24/7
Serverless / pay-per-invocation
On-demand with no autoscaling
Spot, purely because the workload is spiky
items.explanation: Serverless charges only for actual invocations, matching a near-zero baseline with occasional bursts almost exactly. Reserving for the spike would mean paying for idle capacity across all the near-zero hours.
items.reference:
Steady load → reserved · Interruptible → spot · Near-zero baseline → serverless · Otherwise → on-demand + autoscale

Why: the right model depends on predictability and interruption-tolerance, not just listed price.

items.prompt: GreenCart's traffic has a predictable daily floor plus occasional unpredictable sale-driven spikes. What does L2 argue is usually the mistake in a case like this?
choices: Not picking on-demand for everything
Picking a single pricing model for the whole system, instead of blending reserved for the floor and on-demand/serverless for the spikes
Reserving any capacity at all
Using autoscaling instead of a fixed instance count
items.explanation: GreenCart's actual failure was using only on-demand for a workload with a real predictable floor underneath its spikes — the fix isn't switching to a different single model, it's splitting the workload by predictability and applying a different model to each part.
items.reference:
Floor traffic → reserved (predictable, earns the discount)
Spike traffic → on-demand/serverless (unpredictable, no wasted commitment)

Why: most real systems need a blend, not one model for everything.

items.prompt: A system blends reserved capacity for its baseline with autoscaled on-demand for traffic above that baseline. What is this blend optimizing for, that a single-model choice couldn't?
choices: Simplicity of the billing dashboard alone
Paying the discounted rate for the load that's genuinely predictable, while still scaling elastically for the load that isn't
Avoiding on-demand pricing entirely
Guaranteeing zero cost during low-traffic periods
items.explanation: A single model forces a trade-off in one direction: all-reserved wastes money on unpredictable spikes, all-on-demand forfeits the discount available on the predictable floor. The blend captures the discount where it's earned and keeps elasticity where it's needed.
items.reference:
Floor traffic → reserved (predictable, earns the discount)
Spike traffic → on-demand/serverless (unpredictable, no wasted commitment)

Why: most real systems need a blend, not one model for everything.

items.prompt: 'Economies of scale' and 'diseconomies of scale', as used in L2, refer to what specifically?
choices: Whether a company's total revenue is growing or shrinking
Whether cost per unit (per request/order) falls (economies) or rises (diseconomies) as volume grows
Whether a system uses microservices or a monolith
Whether the team's headcount is growing
items.explanation: Both terms in this unit describe the direction of the cost-per-unit curve as volume increases — falling is economies of scale, rising is diseconomies. Neither term is about revenue, team size, or architectural style directly.
items.reference:
Economies of scale → cost/unit falls as volume grows
Diseconomies of scale → cost/unit rises as volume grows

Why: both terms describe the direction of the cost-per-unit curve, nothing else.

items.prompt: In computeMonthlyCost, dbCost is derived from uncachedRequests while onDemandOverflowCost is derived from requestsBeyondReservedCapacity. Why aren't these the same number?
choices: They should be the same number — this is a bug in the code

They track two independent dimensions: whether a request hit the database (the cache dimension) and whether it was covered by committed compute capacity (the capacity dimension) — a request can fall into any combination of the two
uncachedRequests is always larger than requestsBeyondReservedCapacity by definition
Reserved capacity and caching are the same lever, just named differently
items.explanation: cacheHitRatio answers 'did this request need the database?' while reservedCapacityRequestsPerMonth answers 'was this request covered by paid-for compute?' — independent questions about the same request. Treating them as one pool would double-count or miscount requests that land in different combinations.
items.reference:
Cache dimension: hit or miss the DB
Capacity dimension: reserved or on-demand compute
Any request can be either combination independently

Why: two independent dimensions need two independent counts.

items.prompt: A request is served by reserved (already-paid-for) compute capacity, but still misses the cache and reaches the database. Does this request incur onDemandOverflowCost, dbCost, both, or neither?
choices: Both
dbCost only — it's covered by reserved capacity so there's no overflow cost, but it still missed the cache so it still hits the database
onDemandOverflowCost only
Neither — reserved capacity means every downstream cost is free
items.explanation: Being covered by reserved capacity only affects the compute side of the bill, not whether the request hit the cache. The two costs are computed from independent counts, so a reserved-covered, cache-missed request pays dbCost but not onDemandOverflowCost.
items.reference:
Cache dimension: hit or miss the DB
Capacity dimension: reserved or on-demand compute
Any request can be either combination independently

Why: two independent dimensions need two independent counts.

items.prompt: breakEvenUtilization returns reservedRatePerHour / onDemandRatePerHour. If an instance's expected utilization is exactly equal to this ratio, which option is cheaper?
choices: Reserved is strictly cheaper
On-demand is strictly cheaper
Neither — the two options cost the same at exactly the break-even point
The comparison is undefined at that exact point
items.explanation: By construction, the break-even utilization is the exact point where hoursRunPerMonth * onDemandRate equals hoursInMonth * reservedRate — the two costs are equal there, which is why it's called a break-even point rather than a threshold favoring either side.
items.reference:
breakEven = reservedRate / onDemandRate
utilization ≥ breakEven → reserved wins
utilization < breakEven → on-demand wins

Why: a deeper discount doesn't mean reserving is always right — it depends on how often the capacity actually runs.

items.prompt: Given onDemandRatePerHour = $0.10 and reservedRatePerHour = $0.07, what is the break-even utilization, and what does it mean?
choices: 0.7 — reserved is cheaper once the instance runs 70% or more of the month's hours
0.3 — reserved is cheaper below 30% utilization
1.7 — utilization greater than 100% would be required for reserved to win
0.07 — reserved is cheaper below 7% utilization
items.explanation: 0.07 / 0.10 = 0.7. Utilization at or above 70% of the month's hours is where the flat reserved rate starts costing less than paying on-demand only for the hours actually run.
items.reference:
breakEven = reservedRate / onDemandRate
utilization ≥ breakEven → reserved wins
utilization < breakEven → on-demand wins

Why: a deeper discount doesn't mean reserving is always right — it depends on how often the capacity actually runs.

items.prompt: Why does breakEvenUtilization throw a RangeError when onDemandRatePerHour is zero or negative, rather than just returning Infinity or a negative number?
choices: To make the function slower and safer by convention

Because a zero or negative hourly rate isn't a meaningful input — dividing by it would silently produce a nonsensical 'break-even' that could be misread as a real answer instead of the invalid input being flagged
Because JavaScript disallows division by zero entirely and would crash regardless
To match an unrelated convention used elsewhere in the codebase
items.explanation: JavaScript would happily return Infinity or NaN for a division like this rather than crashing — which is exactly the problem: a silent Infinity could get treated as a real utilization threshold downstream. Throwing makes the invalid input impossible to miss.
items.reference:
breakEven = reservedRate / onDemandRate
utilization ≥ breakEven → reserved wins
utilization < breakEven → on-demand wins

Why: a deeper discount doesn't mean reserving is always right — it depends on how often the capacity actually runs.

items.prompt: An instance that only runs during rare sale-day spikes has low expected utilization most months. Per the break-even logic, why would reserving it anyway likely cost MORE than staying on-demand?
choices: Reserved instances are always more expensive in absolute terms than on-demand

The flat reserved rate is paid every month regardless of use, while on-demand at low utilization only charges for the hours actually run — below break-even utilization, on-demand's pay-per-use cost stays lower
Spot pricing is always required for spiky workloads, so reserved is never a valid option
Reserved instances cannot legally be canceled once purchased
items.explanation: Below the break-even utilization, the flat reserved cost exceeds what on-demand would have charged for the same actual usage — the discount doesn't matter if most of the committed hours go unused.
items.reference:
Spike instance ≈ low utilization most months
Reserved cost is flat regardless of use
Below break-even → on-demand wins

Why: a workload's whole reason for existing (rare use) is what makes reserving it a loss.

items.prompt: A team reserves capacity sized for their biggest historical sale-day spike, running it year-round. In a quiet month with no sale, what happens to that instance's effective cost per hour of actual use?
choices: It stays exactly at the reserved hourly rate, no matter how little it's used
It effectively rises, since the same flat monthly cost is being divided across far fewer hours of genuinely useful work
It drops to zero automatically once utilization falls
It becomes identical to the on-demand rate regardless of usage
items.explanation: The reserved rate per billed hour doesn't change, but the *effective* cost per hour of real, useful work rises as fewer of those billed hours are actually doing anything — the same money buying less value in a quiet month.
items.reference:
Spike instance ≈ low utilization most months
Reserved cost is flat regardless of use
Below break-even → on-demand wins

Why: a workload's whole reason for existing (rare use) is what makes reserving it a loss.

items.prompt: recommendTier sizes capacity to peak utilization plus headroom, not average utilization. Why not just size to average, since that's what the instance spends most of its time near?
choices: Average is harder to compute than peak
Sizing to average would leave no slack for the next traffic spike — exactly the failure mode of an under-provisioned system, just discovered later
Peak utilization is always lower than average utilization
Cloud providers only bill based on peak usage anyway
items.explanation: An instance sized to average load is, by definition, undersized for every moment above average — including the busiest moments, when being undersized matters most. Sizing to peak (plus headroom) is what keeps capacity ahead of demand rather than behind it.
items.reference:
Size to average → fails exactly when load is highest
Size to peak + headroom → covers the moments that matter

Why: right-sizing means cheap AND still covers the load actually seen.

items.prompt: An instance's utilization samples show an average of 12% CPU and a peak of 22% CPU during business hours. Which number should drive a right-sizing recommendation, and why?
choices: The average (12%), because most of the time is spent near that level
The peak (22%), plus headroom — sizing below the peak risks the instance being under capacity exactly when load is highest
Neither — right-sizing should ignore CPU entirely and only look at cost
The midpoint between average and peak, as a compromise
items.explanation: The peak is the moment capacity actually gets tested. Sizing below it (as sizing to the 12% average would) means the instance is fine most of the time and under capacity exactly when it matters, which is worse than being slightly oversized the rest of the time.
items.reference:
Size to average → fails exactly when load is highest
Size to peak + headroom → covers the moments that matter

Why: right-sizing means cheap AND still covers the load actually seen.

items.prompt: recommendTier adds a headroomPercent (default 20%) on top of the vCPUs used at peak before picking a tier. What is this headroom protecting against?
choices: Rounding errors in the cost calculation
A future spike slightly larger than anything seen in the sample window, or normal variance, pushing the instance over capacity if it were sized with zero margin above the exact observed peak
The instance being too cheap for the team's budget
Currency conversion differences between regions
items.explanation: The observed peak is only the largest spike seen *so far*. Sizing with zero margin above it assumes the next spike will never be even slightly larger — headroom is the buffer against that assumption being wrong.
items.reference:
Observed peak = largest spike seen SO FAR, not a ceiling

Why: headroom protects against tomorrow's spike being bigger than yesterday's.

items.prompt: Implement `monthlyCostPerRequest(fixedCost, variableCostPerRequest, requests)`: returns `(fixedCost + variableCostPerRequest * requests) / requests`. Throw a `RangeError` if `requests` is 0 or negative.

tests.description: computes cost per request for a normal case
with zero fixed cost, returns exactly the variable cost

items.explanation: This is L2's formula made runnable: the fixed-cost term is divided by requests (diluting as volume grows) and added to the constant variable term. Guarding requests <= 0 matters because dividing by zero or a negative count would silently produce Infinity or a negative 'cost', which is nonsensical and easy to miss downstream if it isn't rejected outright.
items.reference:
costPerRequest = (fixedCost / requests) + variableCostPerRequest

Why: cache hit ratio and reserved capacity are independent dimensions of the same request.

items.prompt: Implement `uncachedRequestCount(totalRequests, cacheHitRatio)`: returns the number of requests that miss the cache, rounded to the nearest whole request (`Math.round(totalRequests * (1 - cacheHitRatio))`). Throw a `RangeError` if `cacheHitRatio` is outside the range 0 to 1 inclusive.

tests.description: computes uncached requests for an 80% hit ratio
with 0% hit ratio, all requests are uncached
